Track: AI Revenue Recovery
Mandate Compliance Scanner — The Problem, The Numbers, The Money
Why a compliance tool belongs on a revenue-recovery track
of banking users trapped in hard-to-cancel subscription flows
encountered interface pressure toward unwanted financial products
RBI's compliance deadline — already passed
1. What the Problem Actually Is

Since February 11, 2026, RBI has had a formal, named definition of "dark pattern" in banking: any interface design that misleads or tricks a user into an action they didn't intend, impairing their autonomy or decision-making. Five specific patterns are now explicitly banned — false urgency (fake countdown timers), pre-checked consent boxes, hidden or hard-to-find cancellation buttons, forced product bundling, and consent flows that let someone agree without being able to actually read the terms. The compliance deadline for all of this was July 1, 2026 — which, as of today, has already come and gone.

This means every bank, NBFC, and by extension every payment flow built on top of them, is currently expected to already be compliant. Most aren't, because the underlying survey data shows just how deeply these patterns are baked into existing products: a 2026 LocalCircles survey of 141,000 respondents across 386 districts found 63% of users hit drip pricing, 61% experienced basket sneaking (unwanted items/products silently added), 68% got stuck in difficult cancellation flows, and 82% felt interface pressure toward products they didn't want.
2. Why This Happens — The Root Cause

This isn't a case of malicious design in most instances — it's a case of nobody auditing UX against a regulation that's only a few months old, applied at a scale where manual review doesn't keep up. India's UPI ecosystem alone processed over 228 billion transactions in 2025, with 45% of that volume from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. At that scale, a subscription or mandate flow was very likely designed and shipped before the February 2026 rule existed, optimized for conversion, not compliance — and nobody has gone back to formally check every screen against the new checklist since. The gap isn't intent, it's the absence of a fast, repeatable audit process, which is exactly what a scanner is for.
3. Why This Is Actually a Revenue Problem, Not Just a Legal One
Three distinct financial mechanisms connect this compliance gap directly to money, not just risk:
Mechanism
How it turns into ₹ impact
Mandatory refund exposure

RBI's draft explicitly requires full refunds in proven mis-selling cases. Every uncompliant flow currently running is accumulating refund liability that doesn't show up on a P&L until a complaint or audit surfaces it — this is a hidden, growing balance-sheet risk, not a one-time fine.
Direct churn from bad UX

68% of users stuck in hard-cancellation flows and 82% feeling pressured are not a compliance statistic in isolation — they are describing exactly the customer experience that damages trust in a recurring-payment relationship. A customer who feels tricked into a mandate is a customer far more likely to actively dispute or cancel at the first opportunity, directly undermining the retention that every other feature in this project is trying to protect.
Enforcement escalation cost

RBI's stated shift from reactive, complaint-based enforcement to proactive, mandatory internal audits means non-compliance is no longer a wait-and-see risk — it's an active audit target. The cost of being caught unaudited (forced remediation under regulatory timeline pressure, reputational damage, potential business restrictions) is far higher than the cost of a routine internal scan.
THE CORE ARGUMENT:

Every other feature in this project (classifier, router, governor) recovers money that's already been lost to a failed payment. This feature is different and complementary — it prevents money from being put at risk in the first place, by catching the exact patterns regulators have said they will now actively audit for.
4. How It's Actually Solved

An LLM-based scanner reads a business's mandate/subscription flow (screen text, consent-checkbox states, cancellation-path structure) against a rulebook built directly from RBI's five named patterns, and returns a structured compliance report: which screens violate which rule, how severe each issue is, and a one-line suggested fix. This was chosen deliberately as an LLM-reasoning task rather than a trained ML model, because the patterns are described qualitatively in the regulation text itself ("false urgency," "hidden opt-out") rather than as statistical features learnable from historical data — and because no labeled dataset of "compliant vs. non-compliant Indian banking UX under this specific 2026 rule" exists or could reasonably be built, since the regulation itself is only months old.
5. What Solving It Actually Delivers
Immediate output:

A structured list of every screen in a mandate/subscription flow that violates one of RBI's five named patterns, with severity and a concrete fix — turning an abstract legal risk into a prioritized action list.
Risk made visible early:
Refund liability that would otherwise accumulate silently until a complaint surfaces it becomes visible and addressable before it becomes a forced, regulator-driven remediation.
A direct link back to the project's core thesis:

A cleaner mandate-setup and cancellation experience is one of the same customer-trust levers the rest of this project depends on — a customer who didn't feel tricked into a subscription is less likely to be a hostile, hard-to-recover churn case later in the pipeline.
6. Where This Sits Relative to the Rest of the Project

This is deliberately scoped as its own standalone service — it needs no output from the classifier, router, or governor, and none of those need anything from it. In the project's overall pitch, it serves as the strongest evidence of independent market research: it's grounded in a regulation that's only months old, backed by a 141,000-respondent survey most competitors won't have cited, and it demonstrates the project understands revenue recovery as "prevent the loss" as well as "recover the loss" — a broader and more complete framing than a pure retry/dunning system alone.
